name: Leather
what: Tanned animal hide, most commonly cattle, also pig, goat and sheep.
note: It's usually described as a waste by-product of the meat industry, but hide has real economic value of its own, so it's more accurate to call it a co-product than pure waste. Tanning is often chrome-tanning, which produces toxic effluent where regulation is weak.
lookFor: Piñatex (pineapple leaf fibre), Mirum, apple leather, cactus leather or mushroom leather, rather than plain "PU leather" - and check the composition, since a lot of cheap "vegan leather" is plain plastic (PU or PVC), which isn't automatically the eco-friendly choice it sounds like.

name: Wool
what: Sheared fleece from sheep, or goats, alpacas and rabbits for cashmere, mohair and angora.
note: This one's genuinely debated even within vegan circles. Some see wool as inherently exploitative, since sheep are bred and confined for human use and typically slaughtered once no longer productive. Others see shearing itself as harmless and focus on specific abuses like mulesing (removing skin from a lamb's rear without anaesthetic, to prevent flystrike). I'm not going to flatten that into a single verdict here - it's worth deciding where you personally land.
lookFor: organic cotton, hemp, TENCEL/lyocell, or recycled polyester fleece for warmth without animal fibre. Recycled wool is still wool, so it doesn't count as an alternative if avoiding wool entirely matters to you.

name: Silk
what: Fibre spun from the cocoons of silkworm larvae.
note: In conventional silk production, cocoons are boiled or gassed with the live pupae still inside, to keep the filament intact. "Peace silk" lets the moth emerge first, avoiding killing, but still farms and confines the insects, so most vegan definitions still exclude it too.
lookFor: "vegan silk" - viscose, satin, or newer lab-grown protein-based alternatives inspired by spider silk.

name: Down & feathers
what: The soft under-plumage of ducks and geese, used for insulation in coats and bedding.
note: Live-plucking (repeatedly pulling feathers from a living bird) is banned under the main certification, the Responsible Down Standard, but investigations have still found it happening on some certified farms. Down is also sometimes a by-product of foie gras farming, which certification is meant to exclude but is hard to fully trace.
lookFor: PrimaLoft, Thermore, or "recycled polyester insulation" - synthetic alternatives now used by plenty of outdoor and coat brands.

name: Fur
what: Pelt with the hair intact, from farmed or trapped animals - mink, fox, chinchilla, rabbit and angora rabbit among them.
note: Fur farming is banned in the UK, but real fur has repeatedly turned up mislabelled as "faux fur" in UK retail, including a well-documented 2017 investigation and a 2019 Advertising Standards Authority ruling against a UK retailer over a jumper's pom-pom (see the brand policy section below for specifics). A "faux fur" label on a cheap item isn't always a guarantee.
lookFor: faux fur from a brand with an actual traceability commitment, or specific fibres like Koba or recycled-polyester faux fur.

name: Exotic skins
what: Leather from snake, crocodile, alligator, lizard or ostrich.
note: These animals are typically farmed, sometimes wild-caught, and welfare investigations have documented animals being skinned while still conscious in some facilities. Several source species are protected under international trade rules (CITES) because of the impact on wild populations.
lookFor: embossed PU, or plant-based leathers like Piñatex finished with a snake or croc-style emboss - there isn't one single common name for this alternative, so it's worth checking the actual material listed.
